title: Greetings and introductions
objectives: I can greet people at different times of the day and say goodbye.
I can introduce myself, ask someone's name and say that I am pleased to meet them.
I can say where I am from and what nationality I am.
I can use the subject pronouns and the present tense of ser.
I can use basic politeness expressions such as por favor, obrigado, desculpa and com licença, and say what each one literally means.
I can explain why each word of this lesson is spelled and accented as it is, using the rules for stress, accents and sounds.

vocabulary.note: The usual informal hello, at any time of day. It is one syllable: the o is the full vowel and the i is a quick glide, like the 'oy' of 'boy'.

A little more careful than oi; common in writing and when speaking to a group. The accent is there because the stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in a: o-LÁ, not O-la. The acute shows an open a, as in 'father'.

Said from waking up until about noon. Bom is the masculine form of 'good' because dia, 'day', is a masculine noun even though it ends in a. The d of dia is said like the j of 'jeans' because it comes before the sound i.

Said from noon until it gets dark. Boa is the feminine form of 'good' because tarde is a feminine noun. Boa has two syllables, bo-a, because two full vowels side by side never form a diphthong. The final e of tarde is weak and sounds like i, so the d before it is said like the j of 'jeans'.

Works as a greeting after dark and as a goodbye. Portuguese has one word, noite, for both English 'evening' and 'night', so one phrase does the work of two. Noite is said NOY-chee: the t comes before the weak final e, which sounds like i.
Said like English 'chow'; an informal goodbye. It is Italian ciao respelled: Portuguese reads ci as 'see', so the sound had to be written tch. The au is a diphthong, so the word has one syllable.

Said when you expect to see the person again before long. Até means 'until' and logo means 'soon'. The accent on até shows that the stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default for e, and that the e is open. The t stays a plain t, because it comes before an open é and not before the sound i.

In amanhã the nh is one sound, like the 'ny' of 'canyon', and the tilde makes the last vowel nasal. The ending ã already defaults to stress on the last syllable, so the tilde needs to do nothing more.

The same two words serve as the question, said with rising intonation, and as the answer. There is no verb. A common reply is Tudo bem, e você? or Tudo ótimo. The m of bem ends the syllable, so the vowel is nasal: bem is said roughly 'bay' through the nose, with no separate n or m sound and the lips left open.

Vai is the third person singular of ir, 'to go', so the question literally asks how it goes. A little more formal than tudo bem. Answer with Bem, obrigado or Bem, obrigada, where bem means 'well'. The ai of vai is a diphthong, one syllable.

Often shortened to prazer. The reply can be prazer too, or o prazer é meu, 'the pleasure is mine'. Prazer is pra-ZER: it ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable by default and no accent is written; the z between vowels is [z]. The ui of muito is said through the nose even though no mark shows it; learn it with the word.

example.target: Muito prazer, eu sou a Ana.
example.source: Nice to meet you, I am Ana.
example.source_literal: Much pleasure, I am the Ana.

vocabulary.note: Por is the small unstressed word 'by, for' and carries no accent; the accented pôr is a different word. Favor ends in r, so it is fa-VOR with no mark.

Said by a man. It is an adjective, so it agrees with the person speaking, not with the person being thanked, because the speaker is the one who is obliged. The br is a tap r and the final o is weak, said 'oo'.
Said by a woman: the feminine form of obrigado, with the same agreement rule. Muito obrigada is literally 'much obliged'.

An informal apology; the more formal form is desculpe. It comes from the verb desculpar, 'to excuse, to forgive', and is a command form of it (commands come later in the course). It is also a polite way to ask someone to repeat what they said. In des-CUL-pa the s ends a syllable, the c before u is [k] and the l that ends a syllable is [w]; in most of Brazil the unstressed e before that s is said like i, so the d sounds like the j of 'jeans'.

Licença means permission, so this phrase asks permission to pass someone, to enter a room or to interrupt politely. It does not apologize; for that you use desculpa. Com ends in m, so the o is nasal. In licença the c before e and the ç before a both say [s].
The reply to obrigado or obrigada. The d of de is said like the j of 'jeans' because the weak final e sounds like i.

Chamar means 'to call' and se is a pronoun meaning 'yourself', so the question says 'how do you call yourself'. A verb used with such a pronoun is called reflexive. Chama is the third person singular, the same form as for ele and ela. Answer with Eu me chamo Ana, literally 'I myself call Ana', or with Meu nome é Ana, 'my name is Ana', where meu is 'my' before a masculine noun. The ch is [ʃ], like 'sh'.

Most country names take the definite article. Brasil is bra-SIL: it ends in l, so the stress is on the last syllable by default and no accent is written. The s between vowels is [z] and the final l is [w], so it sounds like bra-ZEEW. In the example, do is de, 'of', fused with o, 'the'; a later note in this lesson explains the fusion.

Plural, so it takes os, and as a subject it takes a plural verb. Literally 'the states united'. In es-TA-dos the s ends a syllable, and Unidos is u-NI-dos with a plain oral u. In the example, dos is de, 'of', fused with os, 'the'; a later note in this lesson explains the fusion.

example.source: She is from the United States.

vocabulary.note: Feminine: brasileira. Nationalities are written with a lowercase letter. In bra-si-LEI-ro the s between vowels is [z], ei is a diphthong, and the final o is said 'oo'.
Feminine: americana. In Brazil americano usually means from the United States.
The same form for men and women, because adjectives ending in -e have one form for both genders. The en is nasal: ca-na-DEN-se.
Feminine: argentina. The g before e is [ʒ], like the s of 'measure'; the en is nasal; and the t before i is said like 'ch': ar-zhen-CHEE-noo.

From Portugal. Feminine: portuguesa. The accent disappears in the feminine and in the plural portugueses, because por-tu-GUE-sa follows the default for an ending in a. The u after g is silent before ê.
Feminine: francesa. The accent disappears in the feminine for the same reason as in portuguesa. The an is nasal.
A male friend; a female friend is a amiga. The ending shows the gender: -o masculine, -a feminine. In the example, meu is 'my' before a masculine noun.

Este means 'this' before a masculine noun or name; for a woman use esta é, as in Esta é a Ana. The accent on é separates it from the unmarked word e, 'and'. In este the t comes before the weak final e, so it is said like 'ch': ES-chee. In casual speech many Brazilians say esse é instead; that word comes in a later lesson.

Very common in everyday speech: Que legal! means 'How cool!'. Legal comes from the word for law, so it began as 'lawful' and came to mean pleasant or great. Le-GAL ends in l, so the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is written; the g before a is [g] and the final l is [w], so it sounds like leh-GOW.
Built from tam, 'so', and bem, 'well'. Tam-BÉM is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for an ending in em, so the acute accent is written. The em is nasal.

The formal way to say 'you' to a man, used with older people, strangers in formal settings and customers. It takes the same verb form as ele. The nh is [ɲ], like 'ny' in 'canyon', and se-NHOR ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable with no accent.
The formal way to say 'you' to a woman. It takes the same verb form as ela.

example.target: A senhora é de São Paulo?
example.source: Are you from São Paulo, ma'am?
example.source_literal: The lady is of São Paulo?

vocabulary.note: The m ends the syllable, so the i is nasal, [sĩ], and the lips do not close. Often paired with the verb: Sou, sim.

Also the word placed before a verb to make it negative: Eu não sou argentino. The tilde makes the diphthong ão nasal and, with no other accent written, also marks the stress; the word has one syllable.
Ó-ti-mo is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so it always carries an accent; the o is open, so the accent is acute. The t before i is said like 'ch': OH-chee-moo.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stress and accent marks in the words of this lesson
grammar.explanation:
This is the first lesson with real words, so it is where the rules of the previous three lessons start to be used. The principle to hold on to is that a written accent is never decoration. Every word has a stressed syllable, the one said louder and longer than the others, and Portuguese spelling lets you predict it from the last letters of the word. A mark is written only when a word breaks that prediction, or to show a vowel quality or a nasal sound. So when you meet an accent, ask two questions: where would the stress have fallen without it, and what does the mark add?

Take você, the word that puzzles most beginners. Divide it into syllables: vo-cê. The stress is on the last syllable. The default for a word ending in e is the second to last syllable, which would give VO-ce, with a weak final e said 'ee'. Você breaks the default, so a mark must stand on the stressed vowel. The acute accent (´) and the circumflex (^) both mark stress, and they differ in vowel quality: on a, e and o the acute shows an open vowel and the circumflex a closed one (before a nasal m or n the mark is only a spelling convention, as in também, below). The e of você is closed, like the 'ay' of 'say' held steady without the glide, so it takes the circumflex: vo-SAY.

The same reasoning explains the other marked words of this lesson. Olá, até and Canadá are stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in a or e, and their vowels are open, so they take the acute: o-LÁ, a-TÉ, ca-na-DÁ. Português and francês end in es, whose default is the second to last syllable; the stress is on the last syllable and the e is closed, so they take the circumflex: por-tu-GUÊS, fran-CÊS. Também ends in em, whose default is TAM-bem; the stress is on the last syllable, so the acute is written: tam-BÉM. The word é, 'is', is a stressed one-syllable word ending in e, and such words are always marked. The same rule marks nós, 'we', a stressed one-syllable word ending in os, with an open o. The unmarked word e, 'and', is unstressed and said 'ee', which is why é and e are different words.

A second reason for an accent is stress on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts that position, so these words always carry a mark: ótimo (Ó-ti-mo) and México (MÉ-xi-co), both with open vowels and so both with the acute.

The tilde (~) does two jobs. It makes a vowel nasal, and when the word has no other accent it also marks the stress. In são and não the tilde stands over the diphthong ão, a nasal vowel that ends in a w sound, in a single syllable. In amanhã (a-ma-NHÃ) the ending ã already defaults to the last syllable, so the tilde only supplies the nasal sound.

Many words here carry no accent because they follow the default and the ending is enough to read them. Prazer, senhor, favor, legal and Brasil end in r or l, so the stress is on the last syllable: pra-ZER, se-NHOR, fa-VOR, le-GAL, bra-SIL. Tarde, noite, logo, amigo and nome end in a vowel, so the stress is on the second to last syllable. The small word por in por favor is unstressed and unmarked, while pôr, 'to put', is a stressed word whose circumflex tells it apart.

Spelling cannot show one thing: whether an unmarked stressed e or o is open or closed. Ele, 'he', has a closed e and ela, 'she', has an open e; you learn the vowel with the word.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters whose sound depends on their neighbours
grammar.explanation:
A letter's sound in Portuguese is chosen by something you can see: the letter after it, its position in the word, or an accent mark. This note collects every pattern that appears in the words of this lesson and gives the reason for each, so that none of the greetings, nationalities or names is a mystery. Sounds are compared with English, and the symbols in square brackets are phonetic symbols for readers who want to be exact; you can ignore them until they become useful.

Weak final vowels. Most words here end in an unstressed a, e or o, and in Brazilian speech these vowels are weak: a is a short 'uh', o is 'oo' and e is 'ee'. So Ana is AH-nuh, Paulo is POW-loo and tarde is TAR-jee. You write the letter you see and say the weak sound, which is also why the small words a, o and e ('and') are said 'uh', 'oo' and 'ee'.

T and d before i. In most of Brazil a t before the sound [i] is said [tʃ], like the 'ch' of 'cheese', and a d before [i] is said [dʒ], like the 'j' of 'jeans'. The sound [i] means an i and also a weak final e. So noite is NOY-chee, Curitiba has a chee in the middle, ótimo is OH-chee-moo, dia is JEE-uh, de is jee, onde is OHN-jee and tarde is TAR-jee. Before any other vowel t and d are plain: tudo, obrigado, até. Até shows the limit of the rule: its t comes before an open é, which is not the sound [i], so it stays plain. Some regions keep plain t and d everywhere, and you are understood either way.

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by an m or n that ends the syllable is nasal, and the m or n is not said as a separate consonant. In sim, bom, com and bem the lips do not close at the end; the vowel simply flows through the nose. The same happens inside words: canadense, argentino, francês, onde and licença. The tilde does this job in são, não and amanhã. Muito is a special case: nothing in the spelling says so, but its ui is also said through the nose, [ˈmũj̃tu]; learn it with the word.

C, ç, qu, g and gu. The letter c is [k] before a, o and u and [s] before e and i. To write [s] before a, o or u, Portuguese adds a cedilla, giving ç; in licença the c before e and the ç before a both say [s]. To write [k] before e or i, Portuguese writes qu and the u is silent: que is said 'kee'. In the same way gu before e or ê writes [g] with a silent u, as in português. The letter g alone is [g] before a, o and u (legal) and [ʒ], like the s of 'measure', before e and i (argentino). The letter j is always that same [ʒ] sound, whatever vowel follows, as in Janeiro and Rio de Janeiro; j exists so that [ʒ] can be written before a, o and u, where g would say [g].

S. Between two vowels a single s is [z]: brasileiro is bra-zee-LAY-roo, and the z of Souza and prazer is also [z]. At the end of a syllable or word, as in desculpa, Estados, Carlos, nós and francês, the s is [s] in São Paulo and much of the south and [ʃ], 'sh', in the city of Rio de Janeiro.

L at the end of a syllable is [w]: Brasil sounds like bra-ZEEW, legal like leh-GOW and Salvador like sow-va-DOR. An l before a vowel is the l of 'light': Lucas, Lima, Helena, Belo.

R. A strong [h] sound, like a hard English 'h', is written r at the start of a word (Rio, Recife) and rr between vowels. A quick tap of the tongue, like the tt of American 'butter', is written r between vowels or after another consonant in the same syllable: obrigado, prazer. At the end of a syllable (Carlos, senhor, favor) the r depends on the region.

Digraphs and the silent h. A digraph is a pair of letters that spells one sound. Ch is [ʃ], like 'sh' (chama). Nh is [ɲ], like the 'ny' of 'canyon' (amanhã, senhor, senhora). The letter h alone is always silent (Helena, Horizonte). Tchau is a borrowed word: Italian ciao respelled. Portuguese would read ci as 'see', and ch alone is already 'sh', so the sound of English 'ch' is written t plus ch.

Diphthongs. The pairs oi, ai, ei, ou, au and eu are one syllable each, a full vowel followed by a quick glide: oi, vai, brasileiro, Souza, tchau, Paulo, meu. In everyday speech ou is often said as a plain closed o. Two full vowels side by side stay in separate syllables: boa is bo-a. Foreign names keep their own spelling: in Buenos Aires the u is a glide before the e, as if it were written bwe. The x of México is not covered by the pattern for x in the sounds lesson; learn the word, which is said MEH-shee-koo.

grammar.title: Subject pronouns: who is acting
grammar.explanation:
A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun, and a subject pronoun stands in for the noun that performs the action of the verb or is described by it. Grammar sorts subject pronouns by person (the speaker, the listener, anyone else) and by number (one or several), which gives six slots. English fills them with I, you, he or she or it, we, you and they. Notice that English has one word, you, for one listener and for many, and has a word, it, for things. Brazilian Portuguese fills the six slots differently: the listener has a singular and a plural form (você and vocês), there is no word for 'it' as a subject, 'we' has two forms, and the pronoun for the listener behaves grammatically like a third person.

The forms. First person: eu, 'I', written with a lowercase letter unlike English 'I', and nós or a gente, 'we'. Second person, the listener: você for one person and vocês for several. Third person: ele, 'he', and ela, 'she', and in the plural eles and elas. Eles is used for a group of men or a mixed group and elas only for a group of women only, so a single man among a hundred women turns elas into eles. This is the agreement rule from the big-picture lesson: the masculine is the default form of a mixed group.

There is no 'it'. A thing is ele or ela according to its gender only when a pronoun is needed at all, and usually the subject is simply left out: É legal means 'It is cool'.

Why does você take the third person verb? Você began as a respectful way to address someone, Vossa Mercê, 'Your Mercy', a noun phrase about the listener spoken in the third person, like English 'Your Majesty is welcome'. It shrank over the centuries to você but kept its third person verb. So você names the person you are speaking to while being grammatically third person. The formal forms o senhor and a senhora literally mean 'the gentleman' and 'the lady', nouns that are plainly third person. The result is that ele, ela, você, o senhor, a senhora and a gente all take the same verb form.

A gente literally means 'the people', a noun phrase, which is why it takes the third person singular verb even though it means 'we': A gente é de São Paulo. Nós is the careful or written form and takes its own verb form. In everyday speech the two are both common.

Choosing 'you' is a choice about the relationship. Você is the neutral form for one person, used with friends, colleagues and strangers. O senhor and a senhora are more respectful and are used with older people, in service situations and in formal settings. Vocês is the plural in every register. In some regions, including parts of the south, the north and Rio de Janeiro, you will also hear tu for a close friend; you can understand it and never use it, because você is correct everywhere. The choice between você, o senhor and a senhora changes only the word and the tone; the verb stays in the third person in all of them.

Dropping the subject. Because a verb ending shows who is acting, Portuguese often leaves the pronoun out, where English cannot: Sou brasileiro is complete, while English 'am Brazilian' is not. The eu and nós forms have endings of their own (sou, somos), so eu and nós are dropped freely. But é fits six different subjects, so Brazilians usually keep ele, ela or você unless the context already makes it clear. Keep eu when you want to stress it: Eu sou brasileiro, e você?

grammar.title: The verb ser in the present
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has two verbs for 'to be', ser and estar, where English has one. Ser says what something is: identity, origin, nationality and lasting characteristics. Estar, which comes in the next lessons, says how or where something is at the moment. In this lesson ser does three jobs: who someone is (Eu sou a Ana), where they are from (Ela é de Curitiba) and nationality (Ele é brasileiro). Ser is the infinitive, the dictionary form of the verb with no subject and no time. The present tense, shown in the table, is the set of forms for 'now'.

Ser is irregular, which means its forms cannot be built by removing the ending and adding the endings of a regular verb; they must be learned as a block. This is normal for the commonest verb of any language: English am, is and are look just as unrelated to one another. The Portuguese forms are worn-down descendants of the Latin sum, est, sumus and sunt.

Because você, ele, ela, a gente, o senhor and a senhora all take the third person singular, and vocês, eles and elas all take the third person plural, you only need four forms: sou, é, somos and são. English uses three (am, is, are). The form é also serves with no subject at all, where English needs 'it': É legal, 'It is cool'.

Questions. English builds a question by moving the verb ('Are you Brazilian?') or by adding 'do'. Portuguese does neither: the question has the same word order as the statement, said with rising intonation and written with a question mark. Você é brasileiro? and Você é brasileiro. use identical words. A question word goes first, and the verb usually stays where it is: De onde você é? Portuguese answers a yes-or-no question by repeating the verb, so Você é brasileira? Sou. means 'Yes, I am'. Adding sim is also normal: Sou, sim. For no, put não before the verb: Não, eu sou brasileiro.

Sound and spelling. Sou has the diphthong ou, in everyday speech often said as a plain closed o, 'so'. É is an open e, 'eh', and takes the acute accent because it is a stressed one-syllable word (see the first spelling note); the unmarked e means 'and' and is said 'ee': Você é brasileira e ela é americana. Somos is SOH-moos. São ends in the nasal diphthong ão, one syllable, with a w sound at the end.

grammar.title: Saying where you are from and your nationality
grammar.explanation:
To say where you are from, Portuguese uses ser with the preposition de. A preposition is a short word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, and de means 'of' as well as 'from'. The idea is origin: Eu sou de São Paulo literally says 'I am of São Paulo'. English chooses 'from' for this meaning and Portuguese keeps 'of'.

Country names are nouns like any other, with a gender and a number, and most are used with the definite article, 'the': o Brasil, a Argentina, a França, o Canadá, o México, os Estados Unidos. English does this for only a few (the United States, the Netherlands). The ending often shows the gender (a Argentina, a França), but not always (o Brasil, o Canadá, o México), so learn each name with its article. When the preposition de meets the article the two fuse into one word, which is compulsory: de + o = do, de + a = da, de + os = dos. So you say Eu sou do Brasil, Ela é da Argentina and Eles são dos Estados Unidos, never 'de o Brasil'. Portugal has no article, and neither do most cities, so nothing fuses: Ele é de Portugal, Eu sou de Curitiba. A few cities have an article because the name is a common noun; o Rio de Janeiro is the River of January, and rio is masculine, so people say Eu sou do Rio. No rule says which places take an article, so learn each name with it.

A nationality is an adjective, and an adjective agrees with the noun it describes. Here the noun is the person, so the form follows the person's gender, not the country's: a woman from Brazil is brasileira. Most nationalities end in -o for a man and -a for a woman: americano, americana. Those ending in -e, such as canadense, have one form for both. Those ending in a consonant, such as português and francês, usually add -a for the feminine. The accent then disappears, because the new ending a defaults to stress on the second to last syllable and that is where the stress already falls: portuguesa, francesa. The plural adds -s (-es after a consonant), and the accent disappears there too: portugueses, franceses. A mixed group takes the masculine plural. Nationalities are written with a lowercase letter, and in Brazil americano almost always means from the United States.

Two word orders are natural for the question: De onde você é? and Você é de onde?, literally 'Of where you are?' and 'You are of where?'. The verb usually stays in place and no helper word appears.

examples.source: They are from the United States.

grammar.title: Greetings and politeness: what the words literally say and how they are used
grammar.explanation:
Greetings and politeness phrases are fixed formulas. Speakers do not build them word by word, and their natural English equivalents often do not match their words. Two separate questions should be asked of every formula: what do the words literally say, and what do speakers use them for? The literal reading is worth keeping because it explains the grammar inside each formula, and the usage tells you when each one is right. The table gives both, with the natural English between them.

Agreement inside the formulas. Bom dia, boa tarde and boa noite are literally 'good day', 'good afternoon' and 'good night'. Bom and boa are the masculine and feminine forms of the adjective 'good', and each agrees in gender with the noun after it. Dia is masculine even though it ends in a, one of the exceptions to the ending rule; tarde and noite are feminine. So the noun picks the form, not the speaker. Obrigado and obrigada work the other way: the word is the adjective 'obliged', and it agrees with the person speaking, because the speaker is the one who is obliged. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada, whoever is thanked. Muito obrigada is literally 'much obliged'.

Times of day. Bom dia is used from waking until about noon, boa tarde from noon until dark, and boa noite after dark, both as a hello and as a goodbye, because Portuguese has one word, noite, for English 'evening' and 'night'. Oi works at any time and olá is a little more careful. Tchau is a goodbye. Até means 'until', so até logo is 'until soon' and até amanhã is 'until tomorrow'.

Asking how someone is. Tudo bem? is literally 'all well?', with no verb. A Portuguese sentence can leave out the verb when the meaning is clear, and the answer is the same two words, usually followed by e você? Como vai? is literally 'how goes?', with vai from ir, 'to go'; it is a little more formal, and you answer Bem, obrigado, where bem means 'well'.

Meeting someone. Muito prazer is literally 'much pleasure', often shortened to prazer. The reply can be prazer or O prazer é meu, 'the pleasure is mine', where meu is 'my' or 'mine' in the masculine, agreeing with prazer. To give your name, say Eu sou o Carlos or Meu nome é Carlos. In many regions Brazilians put the article before a first name in casual speech (o Carlos, a Ana): names are treated like any noun with a gender, and the article adds no meaning. To ask a name, Como você se chama? literally says 'how you yourself call?'. Chamar means 'to call' and se is a pronoun meaning 'yourself', here standing for você. A verb used with such a pronoun, so that the action comes back to the subject, is called reflexive: Eu me chamo Ana is literally 'I myself call Ana'. Later lessons treat reflexive verbs fully; for now learn the formula. To introduce someone, Este é o Carlos: este means 'this' before a masculine noun, and esta before a feminine one.

Excuse me. English uses one phrase, 'excuse me', for two different acts, and Portuguese separates them. Com licença is literally 'with license', where licença means permission: you ask permission to pass, to enter or to interrupt, which is why it is not an apology. Desculpa is literally 'excuse', from the verb desculpar, 'to excuse, to forgive': you say it after a mistake, or to ask someone to repeat. The formal form is desculpe. Por favor is literally 'for favor', and de nada is literally 'of nothing', a reply that means it was nothing. Que legal! is literally 'what lawful!'; legal began as 'lawful' and now means cool.

examples.target: Muito prazer, eu me chamo Ana.
examples.source: Nice to meet you, my name is Ana.
examples.source_literal: Much pleasure, I myself call Ana.

culture.title: How Brazilians greet each other
culture.text:
Brazilians are warm and physical greeters. Friends and family greet with a hug, and women, and men and women together, often exchange kisses on the cheek. One kiss is common in São Paulo, two in Rio de Janeiro and in many other places, and in parts of Minas Gerais you may get three. Men shake hands or hug. In business settings a handshake is standard the first time you meet.

First names are used almost everywhere, even with your boss or your doctor. Titles still appear with older people and in formal situations: senhor, senhora, and dona before a woman's first name, as in Dona Maria. In some regions you will also hear seu before a man's first name, as in seu João; seu is a short form of senhor.

Tudo bem? works as a greeting even when you are not really asking a question. People often answer Tudo! or Tudo bem, e você? and keep walking. Arriving somewhere, it is polite to greet everyone in the room with a general bom dia or boa tarde before you say anything else.

The choice between com licença and desculpa shows how Portuguese separates two acts that English joins. Asking permission to pass, to enter or to interrupt calls for com licença, while desculpa is for a mistake. A Brazilian who hears desculpa when you only wanted to pass will understand you, but com licença is what a native speaker says.

Finally, Brazilian Portuguese is spoken differently from the Portuguese of Portugal, and you will often hear both accents on the internet. In this course you learn Brazilian forms such as você and a gente.

choices: Boa noite
Boa tarde
Bom dia
exercises.explanation: Boa tarde is used from noon until it gets dark.

exercises.prompt: In você, why is there a circumflex on the e?
choices: It makes the e nasal.
The word is a verb form.
The stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in e, and the e is closed.
It shows that the v is silent.
exercises.explanation: The default for an ending in e is the second to last syllable (VO-ce). Stress on the last syllable needs a mark, and a closed e takes the circumflex where an open e would take the acute.

exercises.prompt: What does the tilde do in são?
choices: It shows that the vowel is open.
It makes the vowel nasal and, since no other accent is written, also marks the stress.
It shows that the s is said [z].
It replaces a missing letter.
exercises.explanation: The tilde marks nasality, and when no other accent is present it also marks the stressed syllable. In são there is only one syllable.

exercises.prompt: What does com licença literally say, word for word?
choices: With license
Excuse me
With apology
I ask pardon
exercises.explanation: Literally 'with license', where licença means permission. 'Excuse me' is the natural English equivalent, not the literal meaning.

exercises.prompt: A woman wants to say 'thank you'. Which word does she use, and why?
choices: Obrigado, because it is the default form.
Obrigado, because she is thanking a man.
Obrigada, because the adjective 'obliged' agrees with the person speaking.
Either one, because it never agrees.
exercises.explanation: Obrigado literally means 'obliged' and agrees with the speaker, not with the person who is thanked.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say bom dia but boa tarde?
choices: Dia is a masculine noun and tarde is a feminine noun, and the adjective agrees with its noun.
Bom is for the morning and boa for later, by custom only.
Boa is more polite than bom.
The speaker's gender decides.
exercises.explanation: Bom and boa are the masculine and feminine of 'good'. Dia is masculine even though it ends in a; tarde and noite are feminine.

exercises.prompt: What sound does tch make in tchau?
choices: The 'sh' of 'shoe'
The 'k' of 'kite'
The 'ch' of 'cheese'
Nothing: it is silent
exercises.explanation: Ch alone is [ʃ], like 'sh'. The t in front gives the 'ch' of English 'cheese'. The word is Italian ciao respelled, because Portuguese reads ci as 'see'.

exercises.prompt: How is the t of noite said, and why?
choices: Like a plain English t, as in 'stop'.
Like the 'ch' of 'cheese', because it comes before the sound i, here the weak final e.
It is silent before e.
Like 'th', because it follows an i.
exercises.explanation: In most of Brazil, t before the sound [i] is [tʃ]. A weak final e sounds like i, so noite is NOY-chee.

exercises.prompt: The t of até is a plain t, although the word ends in e. Why?
choices: Because the word is stressed on the last syllable, which switches the rule off.
Because this e is an open é and not the sound i; only i or a weak final e softens t.
Because t is never soft at the end of a word.
Because the accent is a cedilla.
exercises.explanation: The rule depends on the vowel sound that follows. An open é is not the sound [i].

exercises.prompt: Why is the m of bom not pronounced as a consonant with the lips closed?
choices: Because m is always silent.
Because an m that ends a syllable only makes the vowel before it nasal.
Because bom is a borrowed word.
Because the o is stressed.
exercises.explanation: An m or n that ends a syllable only marks nasality: bom is said [bõ], with the lips open.

exercises.prompt: You need to squeeze past a stranger in a narrow corridor. Which expression fits, and why?
choices: Desculpa, because you have made a mistake.
De nada, because nothing happened.
Com licença, because you are asking permission to pass.
Até logo, because you are leaving.
exercises.explanation: Com licença asks permission (literally 'with license'). Desculpa apologizes for a mistake.

exercises.prompt: Why is ótimo written with an accent, while legal needs none?
choices: Ótimo is longer than legal.
Ótimo is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts; legal ends in l, so the default already puts the stress on the last syllable.
Legal is a borrowed word.
Ótimo is a noun and legal is an adjective.
exercises.explanation: Stress on the third to last syllable is always marked. Words ending in l are stressed on the last syllable by default (le-GAL).

exercises.prompt: Why does português lose its accent in portuguesa?
choices: The ending -a makes the vowel open.
Accents are never written on feminine words.
The new ending a defaults to stress on the second to last syllable, which is where the stress already falls.
The stress moves to the first syllable.
exercises.explanation: Por-tu-GUE-sa: the default for an ending in a already gives the right syllable, so no mark is needed. The same happens in portugueses.

exercises.prompt: Eles são dos Estados Unidos. Why dos and not de os?
choices: Dos is just the plural of de.
De must fuse with the article os, and Estados Unidos is plural and takes os.
Countries never take de.
It is only a spoken shortening and is written de os.
exercises.explanation: A preposition and an article fuse into one word: de + os = dos. The fusion is compulsory in writing too.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun takes the same form of ser as você?
choices: nós
vocês
a gente
eu
exercises.explanation: A gente literally means 'the people', a third person noun phrase, so it takes é like você, ele and ela.
Sou is the eu form of ser. Only eu takes sou.
Somos is the nós form of ser.
A gente means 'we' but is grammatically third person singular, so the verb is é, not somos.
Vocês, eles and elas share the form são.
De + o fuses into do, because o Brasil takes the article o.
De + a fuses into da, because a Argentina takes the article a.
The nationality agrees with the person: a woman is brasileira.
Francês adds -a for the feminine and loses its accent, because the ending a already puts the stress on the right syllable.

exercises.prompt_target: O Carlos e a Ana são ___.
exercises.explanation: A mixed group takes the masculine plural.
Dia is masculine, so the adjective is bom. With tarde or noite it would be boa.

exercises.hint_source: Thank you very much! (said by a woman)
exercises.explanation: Obrigada is 'obliged' in the feminine, agreeing with the woman speaking.
The subject pronoun can be dropped, and the article before the name is optional.

exercises.prompt_source: Where are you from? (to a friend)
exercises.explanation: These word orders are natural. No helper word is needed.
De + a fuses into da before a feminine country name.

exercises.prompt_source: We are Brazilian. (a group of men)
exercises.explanation: Nós takes somos and the plural brasileiros. A gente is singular in form, so its verb is é, and in everyday speech the adjective usually stays singular.
Elas is for women only; francês becomes francesa, plural francesas.
México takes the masculine article o, so de + o gives do.

exercises.prompt_source: We are from the United States.
exercises.explanation: Estados Unidos is plural and takes os, so de + os gives dos.

choices: Good afternoon, how are you?
Good morning, how are you?
Good night, see you tomorrow.
She is French.
They are French.
We are French.
exercises.explanation: São is the plural form, and elas is the plural of ela.

choices: She is Canadian.
She is Brazilian.
She is American.
I am from Brazil.
I am from Argentina.
I am from Mexico.
A woman says thank you and hears you're welcome.
A man says thank you and hears you're welcome.
Someone says sorry and hears it is fine.
exercises.explanation: Obrigada is the feminine form, so the speaker is a woman.
Check the tch, the acute on até and the nh and tilde of amanhã.
Check the circumflex on você and on português.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its literal, word-for-word meaning
exercises.explanation: The literal meaning shows the grammar inside each formula; the natural English equivalents are excuse me, you're welcome, see you later, how's it going and thank you.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the spelling rule that explains it

pairs.source: circumflex: stress on the last syllable, closed e
tch spells the ch of cheese
nh spells the ny of canyon
final m makes the vowel nasal

exercises.explanation: Each mark or letter group has one fixed job.
